subject: biology
title: Water movement through the plant
key_idea: Water enters a plant through root hair cells, crosses the root cortex, rises up the xylem and leaves as vapour through the stomata. Evaporation from the leaf pulls up a column of water held together by cohesion. A plant that loses water faster than it takes it up wilts.

sections.heading: The route of water through the plant

blocks.text: Water travels from the soil to the air through the root, stem and leaf. This section gives the pathway in order.

diagram.alt: The pathway of water through a plant in order: root hair cell, root cortex cells, xylem, mesophyll cells, air spaces in the leaf, then out through the stomata.
diagram.prompt: Put the pathway of water through the plant in order, from the soil to the air.
steps: Root hair cells take in water from the soil by osmosis
Water crosses the root cortex cells
Water rises through the xylem in the stem
Water leaves the xylem and enters the mesophyll cells in the leaf
Water evaporates into the air spaces and diffuses out of the stomata

items: Root hair cells have a large surface area, so they take in water quickly.
The **xylem** is a continuous tube of dead cells with no end walls. It carries water and mineral ions up the plant.
In the leaf, water moves from the xylem into the **mesophyll** cells.
The pathway is root hair cells, root cortex cells, xylem, mesophyll cells.
Water enters root hair cells by osmosis.

sections.heading: Tracing the pathway with a stain

blocks.text: A stain shows which part of the stem carries water. The method is the same for any leafy shoot.

items.text: Cut the stem of a leafy plant, for example celery, under water.
Stand the cut stem in water containing a coloured dye, such as eosin or red ink.
Leave it for several hours, so water is drawn up the stem.
Cut thin slices across the stem and lengthways.
The dye is found in the xylem, which shows where water travels.

items: A coloured dye in the water shows the pathway in the stem.
The stain is found in the xylem.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Water is lost from a leaf as vapour. This section covers how the leaf is built for this.

items.meaning: The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant.
Small pores in the leaf, mostly on the underside, which let gases and water vapour pass.

items: Water **evaporates** from the surface of the mesophyll cells into the air spaces.
The air spaces between mesophyll cells interconnect and give a large internal surface area.
Water vapour diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata.
More and larger stomata mean more water vapour is lost.
Water evaporates from mesophyll cells into the air spaces.
Vapour escapes by diffusion through the stomata.
A large internal surface area and more stomata increase water loss.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Water moves up the xylem without a pump. Evaporation from the leaf does the work.

items: Water evaporates from the leaf, so the pressure at the top of the xylem falls.
This **transpiration pull** draws up a column of water in the xylem.
Water molecules are held together by forces of attraction between them. This is **cohesion**.
The xylem is a continuous tube, so the column does not break.
Water molecules also stick to the walls of the xylem (adhesion).
If water is lost faster than the roots take it up, the cells lose water.
The cells lose their firmness and become limp, or **flaccid**.
Nothing pushes the cell contents against the cell wall, so the leaves and stems droop.
This is **wilting**. It happens in hot, dry or windy conditions, or when the soil is dry.
Wilting reduces the surface area exposed, so less water is lost.
Transpiration pull draws up a column of water molecules held together by cohesion.
Wilting happens when water loss is greater than water uptake.

checks.q: Name the tissue that carries water up the stem.
Describe how you could show which part of a stem carries water.
checks.a: Stand a cut stem in water with a coloured dye. After some time, cut a thin slice of the stem. The dye is seen in the xylem.

checks.q: (Supplement) Explain how water moves up the xylem.
checks.a: Water evaporates from the leaf, causing transpiration pull. This draws up a column of water in the xylem. The water molecules stay together because of forces of attraction between them (cohesion).

worked_example.question: Describe how water moves through a plant from the soil to the air spaces in a leaf.
answer_points: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis.
It moves through the root cortex.
It reaches the xylem in the root.
A column of water moves up the stem in the xylem.
Water molecules are held together by forces of attraction (cohesion).
Water moves out of the xylem in the leaf into the mesophyll cells.
Water evaporates from the surface of the mesophyll cells into the air spaces.
